metadata.methods_description: Participants completed two three-minute trials for each terrain and speed condition, plus a three-minute seated rest trial. Recordings comprised dual-layer EEG, neck EMG, IMU acceleration, and ground reaction forces. Digitized electrode locations and T1 structural MRI were used to construct head models.

citation_details.title: Age differences in electrocortical dynamics during uneven terrain walking
citation_details.author: Chang Liu, Erika M. Pliner, Jacob S. Salminen, Ryan J. Downey, Jungyun Hwang, Arkaprava Roy, Ryland D. Swearinger, Natalie Richer, Chris J. Hass, David J. Clark, Todd Matthew Manini, Yenisel Cruz‐Almeida, Rachael D. Seidler, Daniel Perry Ferris
citation_details.abstract: Walking on uneven terrain becomes more difficult as we age, and gait becomes less automatic. Using mobile brain imaging via high-density electroencephalography (EEG) can provide insight into the neural mechanisms contributing to reduced mobility capability with aging. The objective of this study was to quantify age differences in electrocortical dynamics during uneven terrain walking, both averaged across many strides and variations within a stride. We included 31 young adults and 71 older adults for analysis. All participants walked on an uneven terrain treadmill with four levels of terrain difficulty at their self-selected speed. Compared to younger adults, older adults exhibited a greater increase in step duration variability and mediolateral sacral excursion variability as the terrain became more uneven. We identified multiple brain regions involved during walking on uneven terrain. Regardless of age group, walking on uneven terrain compared to flat terrain led to a widespread change of electrocortical dynamics in the brain, especially in the alpha (8-13Hz) and beta (13-30Hz) band power. In the parieto-occipital region, younger adults experienced a greater reduction in alpha and beta power with increasing terrain unevenness compared to older adults. We also assessed how intra-stride power fluctuations changed with terrain unevenness and age group. Greater intra-stride power spectral fluctuations in the occipital area were associated with greater terrain unevenness for younger adults, but not for older adults. In summary, older adults showed a greater increase in gait variability than younger adults as the terrain became more uneven, but exhibited a lack of modulation of parieto-occipital activity in response to terrain unevenness. The lack of task-related power modulation may suggest reduced cortical network flexibility in older adults. The absence of increased parieto-occipital activity when walking on uneven versus flat surfaces in older adults may also indicate that, unlike younger adults, older adults already heavily rely on visual processes during flat surface walking and may therefore have reduced occipital modulation range remaining to cope with the visuomotor processing demands of walking on uneven surfaces.

citation_details.title: Compensation Related Utilization of Neural Circuits Hypothesis (CRUNCH) of Electrocortical Data during Walking on Uneven Terrain
citation_details.author: Erika M. Pliner, Chang Liu, Jacob S. Salminen, Patricia A. Reuter‐Lorenz, Ryland D. Swearinger, Jungyun Hwang, Arkaprava Roy, Natalie Richer, David J. Clark, Todd Matthew Manini, Chris J. Hass, Yenisel Cruz‐Almeida, Rachael D. Seidler, Daniel Perry Ferris
citation_details.abstract: Mobility limitations are common in older age, but the association of age-related changes in the neural control of walking are not well understood. We investigated whether the Compensation Related Utilization of Neural Circuits Hypothesis (CRUNCH) – a model that describes age differences in brain activity with increasing cognitive demand – applies to walking under varying levels of task difficulty. We assessed the electrocortical data of younger and older adults walking on a treadmill with varied levels of uneven terrain (i.e., varying difficulty levels). We observed CRUNCH effects in the posterior parietal regions, which are thought to be associated with planned movements, spatial reasoning, and attention. We found older adults displayed greater alpha desynchronization than younger adults at low terrain unevenness, and younger adults displayed greater range in utilized spectral power in the alpha band across levels of terrain unevenness than older adults. These results demonstrate both over-recruitment and ceiling effects, respectively, of neural resources in older adults compared to younger adults, as predicted by the CRUNCH model. These findings provide novel insights into age differences in the neural control of mobility and may lead to new interventions for maintaining function in older age.

citation_details.title: Where Does EEG Help Wearable Freezing of Gait Detection?
citation_details.author: Chuntian Chi, Lifang He, Huajie Shao, Gang Zhou
citation_details.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) detectors built on inertial measurement units (IMUs) are accurate while the legs move, but they become unreliable when the legs are nearly still, which is exactly when akinetic freezing, voluntary stopping, and standing must be told apart. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures motor-planning activity that leg sensors cannot, but EEG is impractical for daily use. We ask where EEG helps: as an input at inference time, or only during pretraining, so that the deployed detector still needs only IMUs. We assemble a pretraining corpus of synchronized EEG and IMU recordings (5 datasets, 184 people, 94 hours) and compare six settings that differ only in the modalities used for pretraining and as model input, each with tuned hyperparameters and five independent pretraining runs. On the BXHC FoG dataset (leave-one-patient-out, 10 patients with FoG), adding EEG as input raises FoG F1 from 0.663 to 0.740 (9 of 10 patients improve), and the gain in ranking performance is confined to the quartile of windows with the least leg movement (AUROC +0.063). Pretraining the IMU encoder jointly with EEG improves an IMU-only detector both within the cohort (FoG F1 0.663 to 0.705) and when it is trained on a small cohort and tested on another (FoG F1 +0.083, all 10 test patients improve). Repeating the study with PD-only and healthy-only pretraining corpora, each with its own hyperparameter search, shows that IMU-based detection is robust to the corpus, whereas the benefit of aligning EEG with IMU requires both. Cross-cohort analysis further shows that detectors trained without annotated voluntary stops classify nearly all stops as freezing. Finally, on PD versus non-PD classification in three external datasets, joint EEG+IMU pretraining improves PD detection from walking EEG over EEG-only pretraining (AUROC 0.750 vs. 0.683), while IMU-based detection does not depend on the pretraining.
